metadata.scope: e_suvarnabhumi (all 180 baronies across k_dvaravati and k_pagan)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_haripunjaya.first_mention_attestation: Dated Old Mon stone inscriptions from Lamphun (1213, 1218, and 1219 CE, Wat Don LPh. 01), with undated Old Mon epigraphy beginning c. 11th century CE; late chronicles (Camadevivamsa [15th c. CE], Jinakalamali [1516 CE]) retroject a 662/663 CE foundation.
b_haripunjaya.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Pali Haripuñjaya (also Haribhuñjaya), a classical Indic name borne by the Mon kingdom centered at Lamphun. Although archaeological remains in the Lamphun basin predate 867 CE and 15th–16th century CE Pali chronicles (Camadevivamsa, Jinakalamali) claim a 7th-century CE foundation by Queen Camadevi of Lavo, the earliest contemporary epigraphic attestations date to the 11th–13th centuries CE (with dated Lamphun steles from 1213 CE onward), so it is not contemporarily attested by 867 CE.

b_chiang_mai.first_mention_attestation: Founded by King Mangrai of Lan Na in 1296 CE as Nopburi Si Nakhon Ping Chiang Mai (Lanna inscriptions and chronicles).
b_chiang_mai.etymology_analysis: Northern Thai Chiang ('walled city') + Mai ('new'), founded in 1296 CE by King Mangrai as the new capital of Lan Na. Later chronicles mention a prior Lawa settlement called Wiang Nopburi, but this has no contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation.

b_chom_thong.first_mention_attestation: Mid-15th century CE (c. 1451 CE) construction of Wat Phra That Si Chom Thong Worawihan in Chiang Mai province.
b_chom_thong.etymology_analysis: From Thai/Northern Thai Chom ('peak, summit') + Thong ('gold'), referring to the hill Doi Chom Thong and the mid-15th century CE temple Wat Phra That Si Chom Thong. No contemporary <= 867 CE attestation exists.

b_phrao.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Lan Na historical tradition as named by King Mangrai around 1281 CE during his campaign against Haripuñjaya.
b_phrao.etymology_analysis: Northern Thai/Thai Phrao ('coconut'). Named around 1281 CE under King Mangrai of Lan Na, well after the 867 CE baseline.

b_hlaingbwe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; appears in late colonial-era Kayin chronicles and 19th-century CE Burmese administrative records.
b_hlaingbwe.etymology_analysis: Town in Kayin State, Myanmar, named directly after the Hlaingbwe River (from Karen hlaing 'water' + bwe 'to flow around a hill'). No contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation exists.

b_mueang_tak.first_mention_attestation: Ramkhamhaeng Inscription (Sukhothai Inscription No. 1, 1292 CE), which records Khun Sam Chon of Mueang Chot attacking Mueang Tak.

morphemes.translation: to dry in the sun / Tak

b_mueang_tak.etymology_analysis: Thai Mueang ('walled town, principality') + Tak. First contemporarily attested in the 1292 CE Ramkhamhaeng Inscription; later chronicle traditions linking it to 7th-century CE Takkasila are retrospective and not contemporarily attested <= 867 CE.

b_mae_sot.first_mention_attestation: Identified with Mueang Chot in the Ramkhamhaeng Inscription (1292 CE); the modern name Mae Sot appears in 19th-century CE Siamese records.
b_mae_sot.etymology_analysis: Named after the Mae Sot (Huai Mae Sot) stream, with Thai Mae ('mother', used for rivers) + Sot. Often identified with Mueang Chot of the 1292 CE Ramkhamhaeng Inscription, but unattested <= 867 CE.

b_hot.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; appears in post-867 CE Lan Na and Siamese administrative records (also known as Tha Kham).
b_hot.etymology_analysis: Northern Thai/Thai Hot (from Northern Thai 'to reach, arrive'). A district town in southern Chiang Mai province with no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_mae_hong_son.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1831 CE as a wild-elephant capture and training camp ordered by the ruler of Chiang Mai.
b_mae_hong_son.etymology_analysis: Named after the Mae Hong Son stream (Shan/Northern Thai Mae 'river' + Hong Son 'stream where elephants are trained'). Founded in 1831 CE and granted city status in 1874 CE, well after 867 CE.

b_pai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; local history traces settlement to Ban Wiang Nuea c. 13th century CE, with Pai appearing in 19th-century CE Lanna/Siamese records.
b_pai.etymology_analysis: Takes its name directly from the Pai River (locally linked to Northern Thai chang pai 'male elephants' or a Shan term). No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_karen.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; the ethnonym Karen (Burmese Kayin) is first documented in 18th-century CE Burmese and European records.
b_karen.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym referring to the Karenic-speaking peoples of Lower Myanmar and western Thailand (anglicized from Burmese Kayin). Not contemporarily attested as a polity or settlement <= 867 CE.

b_khu_bua.first_mention_attestation: Modern Thai name Khu Bua ('lotus moat') is unattested <= 867 CE; the underlying 7th-century CE (c. 650 CE) Dvaravati urban center in Ratchaburi yielded Pallava-script silver medallions inscribed śrī-dvāravatī-īśvara-puṇya ('the merit of the glorious lord of Dvāravatī') and contemporary Buddhist monuments.
b_khu_bua.etymology_analysis: Modern Thai compound Khu Bua ('lotus moat'), referring to the moated Dvaravati archaeological site in Ratchaburi; while the site itself is a major 7th-century CE Dvaravati center, the Thai toponym Khu Bua is not attested <= 867 CE.

b_uthai_thani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; named Uthai Thani in the late 18th century CE under King Taksin (r. 1767–1782 CE).
b_uthai_thani.etymology_analysis: From Pali-derived Thai Uthai ('dawn, sunrise') + Thani ('city'). Although Dvaravati-era artifacts exist in the province, the town of Uthai Thani itself has no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_mueang_sing.first_mention_attestation: Late 12th–early 13th century CE Angkorian temple complex (identified with Śrī Jaya Siṃhapura in the 1191 CE Preah Khan inscription); Thai name Mueang Sing appears in King Rama I's chronicles (1782–1809 CE).
b_mueang_sing.etymology_analysis: Thai Mueang ('town') + Sing (from Sanskrit siṃha 'lion'), reflecting the Khmer-period city name Siṃhapura. Built in the Bayon style (late 12th–13th century CE), postdating the 867 CE baseline.

b_lop_buri.first_mention_attestation: 7th–8th century CE (c. 650 CE) silver coins inscribed Lavapura in Pallava script (recovered in the 1966 U Thong hoard).
b_lop_buri.etymology_analysis: Modern Thai form of Sanskrit/Pali Lavapura ('city of Lava/Lavo'), contemporarily attested on 7th–8th century CE Pallava-script silver coins as a major Dvaravati/Lavo center.

b_chan_sen.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; known archaeologically as a moated Dvaravati settlement (c. 600–1000 CE) in Nakhon Sawan.
b_chan_sen.etymology_analysis: Modern Thai name (Chan 'sandalwood/moon' + Sen 'hundred thousand') of an archaeological Dvaravati moated town in Takhli District, Nakhon Sawan. Despite 1st-millennium CE archaeological occupation, it lacks contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic or chronicle attestation by name.

b_sri_thep.first_mention_attestation: 6th–7th century CE Sanskrit inscription K. 978 (issued by King Bhavavarman in Pallava script) found at Si Thep, alongside 6th–7th century CE Dvaravati monuments.
b_sri_thep.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Śrī Deva ('auspicious deity'), one of the largest first-millennium CE Dvaravati city-states in the Pa Sak valley, contemporarily attested by the 6th–7th century CE Sanskrit inscription K. 978.

b_nakhon_pathom.first_mention_attestation: The Pali-derived name Nakhon Pathom (Nagara Paṭhama, 'First City') was bestowed by King Mongkut (Rama IV, r. 1851–1868 CE) in the mid-19th century CE (restoration begun 1853 CE) on the ancient Dvaravati capital.
b_nakhon_pathom.etymology_analysis: From Pali Nagara Paṭhama ('first city'), a name bestowed by King Mongkut (Rama IV) in the 19th century CE on the ancient Dvaravati capital (attested in 6th–7th century CE inscriptions, silver coins, and Tang Chinese records as Dvāravatī).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 6th-century CE Wat Phra Ngam Pallava-script Sanskrit inscription; 7th-century CE silver coins (Śrī Dvāravatīśvara puṇya); Xuanzang's Da Tang Xiyu Ji (648 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Dvaravati capital attested <= 867 CE as Dvāravatī / Duoluobodi prior to the 19th-century CE naming Nakhon Pathom.

b_bangkok.first_mention_attestation: Early 15th-century CE Ayutthaya-era riverside trading post recorded as Bang Makok; founded as Siam's capital in 1782 CE.
b_bangkok.etymology_analysis: Shortened from Thai Bang Makok ('village of hog plums', Spondias pinnata), first attested as an Ayutthaya-period settlement in the early 15th century CE, long after 867 CE.

b_ayuthia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1351 CE by King Ramathibodi I (U Thong) as the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom (preceded by 11th–13th century CE Ayodhya).
b_ayuthia.etymology_analysis: Named after the sacred Indian city of Ayodhyā (Sanskrit 'unconquerable, invincible'). Founded in 1351 CE on an island at the confluence of the Chao Phraya, Pa Sak, and Lopburi rivers, postdating 867 CE.

b_u_thong.first_mention_attestation: Modern Thai name U Thong ('cradle of gold') is unattested <= 867 CE; the underlying moated Dvaravati site yielded the mid-7th century CE Sanskrit copper-plate inscription of King Harṣavarman (K. 964) and 7th-century CE Dvaravati silver coins.
b_u_thong.etymology_analysis: Modern Thai compound U ('cradle') + Thong ('gold'), applied to an early Dvaravati urban center in Suphan Buri that yielded the mid-7th century CE Sanskrit copper-plate inscription K. 964 and 7th-century CE silver coinage; the Thai toponym U Thong itself is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_chiang_khaeng.first_mention_attestation: 15th-century CE foundation of the Tai Lue principality of Chiang Khaeng (Kengcheng) on the upper Mekong.
b_chiang_khaeng.etymology_analysis: Tai Lue/Shan Chiang ('walled city') + Khaeng. Founded as a Tai Lue principality in the 15th century CE, well after the 867 CE baseline.

b_moeng_phong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented in 19th-century CE Tai Lue chronicles (Phongsawadan Muang Chiang Rung) and Qing sources as a Sipsongpanna principality.
b_moeng_phong.etymology_analysis: Tai Lue Moeng ('principality, valley polity') + Phong (Möng Hpawng / Mengpeng in Sipsongpanna). No contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation exists.

b_pak_beng.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Lao historical tradition in connection with King Fa Ngum's 1353 CE unification of Lan Xang.
b_pak_beng.etymology_analysis: Lao Pak ('mouth of a river') + Beng (the Nam Beng river), a locator compound denoting the confluence of the Nam Beng with the Mekong. No contemporary <= 867 CE attestation exists.

b_luang_prabang.first_mention_attestation: Ramkhamhaeng Inscription (1292 CE, listing Luang Prabang across the Mekong as Sukhothai's northern limit); late Lao chronicles retroject Muang Sua to the 8th century CE.
b_luang_prabang.etymology_analysis: Lao Luang ('royal, great') + Phra Bang (the sacred Buddha image brought from Angkor in the 14th century CE). Earlier names Muang Sua and Xieng Dong Xieng Thong appear in late Lao chronicles, but lack contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic or external-chronicle attestation.

b_sainyabuli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; documented as western Lan Xang territory (post-1353 CE) and organized administratively in the 19th–20th centuries CE.
b_sainyabuli.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Pali Jayapurī ('city of victory'), adapted into Lao as Sainyabuli (Xayaburi). No contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation exists.

b_muang_ngoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; riverine settlement on the Nam Ou in Luang Prabang province documented in modern Lao administrative records.
b_muang_ngoi.etymology_analysis: Lao Muang ('town, district') + Ngoi. A settlement on the Nam Ou river in northern Laos with no contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation.

b_muang_souy.first_mention_attestation: Predecessor village Ban Nong Tang existed from c. 1900 CE; the town of Muang Soui (Muang Souy) was created shortly before 1960 CE.
b_muang_souy.etymology_analysis: Lao Muang ('town, district') + Souy (Muang Soui) in Xiangkhouang Province, Laos, established in the 20th century CE (replacing Ban Nong Tang, attested from 1900 CE).

b_nan.first_mention_attestation: Ramkhamhaeng Inscription (1292 CE, listing Nan among northern polities); west-bank city founded in 1368 CE. Rattanakosin-era Ratchawongsapakon retrojects a 677 CE lineage.
b_nan.etymology_analysis: Shortened from Nanthaburi (Pali Nanda 'joy' + purī 'city'). Contemporarily attested from the 1292 CE Ramkhamhaeng Inscription; the 677 CE date in the late Rattanakosin-period Ratchawongsapakon chronicle is retrospective.

b_muang_thong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern Lao settlement/district name (Thongmixay / Muang Thong in Sainyabuli Province).
b_muang_thong.etymology_analysis: Lao/Tai Muang ('town, principality') + Thong ('gold, golden'). No contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation exists.

b_chiang_klang.first_mention_attestation: 15th-century CE Northern Thai chronicles (Nan flourishing under the name Chiang Klang, between Chiang Mai and Chiang Thong)
b_chiang_klang.etymology_analysis: From Northern Thai Chiang (a Sino-Tai loanword meaning walled city or fort) + Klang (middle, central), referring to Nan's 15th-century CE position midway between Chiang Mai and Chiang Thong (Luang Prabang). No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_chiang_saen.first_mention_attestation: Founded 1327–1329 CE by King Saen Phu of Lan Na (Northern Thai chronicles; early Lan Na epigraphy begins 1370 CE at Wat Phra Yün); Yonok/Ngoenyang legends claiming 545 CE or 850 CE are late retrospective chronicles
b_chiang_saen.eponym_details: Named after King Saen Phu of Lan Na (r. 1325–1334 CE), grandson of King Mangrai, who founded Chiang Saen in 1327–1329 CE.

morphemes.translation: Saen Phu (personal name, literally hundred thousand)

b_chiang_saen.etymology_analysis: From Northern Thai Chiang (walled city) + Saen (after founder King Saen Phu, 1327–1329 CE). Earlier Yonok and Ngoenyang traditions claiming 6th–9th century CE dates derive solely from late retrospective chronicles without contemporary pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation.

b_mong_hang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; documented as a Shan valley settlement in eastern Shan State only in modern-era records
b_mong_hang.etymology_analysis: From Shan Mong (valley principality or town) + Hang (tail, end). No contemporary pre-867 CE epigraphic, numismatic, or chronicle attestation exists.

b_chiang_rai.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1262 CE by King Mangrai as the capital of Ngoenyang/Lan Na (Northern Thai chronicles; early Lan Na epigraphy from 1370 CE onward)
b_chiang_rai.eponym_details: Named after King Mangrai (1238–1311 CE), who founded Chiang Rai in 1262 CE and later established the Lan Na Kingdom.
b_chiang_rai.etymology_analysis: From Northern Thai Chiang (walled city) + Rai (abbreviated from founder King Mangrai, 1262 CE). Post-867 CE foundation with no contemporary pre-867 CE attestation.

b_chiang_rung.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1180 CE by Tai Lü ruler Phanya Coeng (Pa Zhen) as Chiang Hung (Mueang Ho Kham Chiang Rung); later attested in Yuan dynasty records as Cheli
b_chiang_rung.etymology_analysis: From Tai Lü Chiang (walled city) + Rung / Hung (dawn), meaning City of Dawn, founded in 1180 CE as the capital of Sipsongpanna (modern Jinghong). Post-867 CE foundation.

b_mong_la.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; emerged as a Tai Lü muang (Mengla) within the Sipsongpanna (Cheli) confederation in the post-1180 CE era
b_mong_la.etymology_analysis: From Tai Lü Mong (valley principality) + La (tea), meaning tea-producing principality (modern Mengla County, Xishuangbanna). No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_chiang_coeng.first_mention_attestation: 15th-century CE (c. 1400 CE) foundation of the Tai Lü principality of Chiang Khaeng (Kengcheng) on the upper Mekong, later recorded in 1558 CE when conquered by King Bayinnaung of Toungoo Burma.
b_chiang_coeng.etymology_analysis: From Tai Lü Chiang (walled city) + Coeng / Khaeng (strong, firm), referring to the Tai Lü principality of Chiang Khaeng (Kengcheng) on the Mekong. No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_moeng_hing.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE sources; Tai Lü/Shan toponym in the Sipsongpanna region only documented in later periods
b_moeng_hing.etymology_analysis: From Tai Lü Moeng (valley principality) + Hing (bell or side/ginger). No contemporary pre-867 CE epigraphic or chronicle attestation exists.

b_moeng_cae.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Qing-era Sipsongpanna confederation (Jingzhen Octagonal Pavilion built 1701 CE in Mengzhe/Moeng Cae; documented as Moeng Cae in 1888 CE)
b_moeng_cae.etymology_analysis: From Tai Lü Moeng (valley principality) + Cae (to soak in water), referring to the water-soaked basin of Mengzhe (Xishuangbanna). No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_moeng_long.first_mention_attestation: 1204 CE (565 in the Dai calendar) Buddhist record of Manfeilong Pagoda sponsored by the chieftain of Menglong (Moeng Long) in Sipsongpanna
b_moeng_long.etymology_analysis: From Tai Lü Moeng (valley principality) + Long (great, large), meaning Great Principality (modern Menglong in Jinghong, Xishuangbanna). Post-867 CE attestation.

b_muang_u.first_mention_attestation: 1750 CE earliest Kongdin boundary documents from Phongsaly Province, northern Laos (no written sources in the region predate the 18th century CE)
b_muang_u.etymology_analysis: From Lao Muang (valley principality) + U (the Nam Ou river, where Muang Ou Neua and Muang Ou Tai lie at the headwaters). Written records in Phongsaly begin only in the 18th century CE.

b_muang_sing.first_mention_attestation: 1885 CE when the capital of Chiang Khaeng was transferred to Muang Sing (incorporated into French Laos in 1904 CE)
b_muang_sing.etymology_analysis: From Lao Muang (valley principality) + Sing (from Sanskrit siṃha, lion). Established as a seat only in the late 19th century CE, with no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_chiang_tong.first_mention_attestation: 1243 CE establishment of Kengtung (Chiang Tung) State in regional Shan/Tai Khün historical records (reestablished in the late 13th century CE by Mangrai's grandson)
b_chiang_tong.etymology_analysis: From Tai Khün Chiang (walled city) + Tong / Tung (classical Pali/Sanskritized Tungapuri). Post-867 CE foundation with no contemporary pre-867 CE attestation.

b_chakangrao.first_mention_attestation: 1376–1388 CE Ayutthaya attacks on Chakangrao (ancient Kamphaeng Phet) recorded in Sukhothai and Ayutthaya historical records
b_chakangrao.etymology_analysis: Old Thai toponym Chakangrao, the 14th-century CE Sukhothai-era name for the fortified city on the east bank of the Ping River that became Kamphaeng Phet. No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_kamphaeng_phet.first_mention_attestation: 1510 CE dedicatory inscription on a bronze Śiva statue naming Śrī Dharmāśokarāja, prince of Kamphaeng Phet
b_kamphaeng_phet.etymology_analysis: From Thai Kamphaeng (wall, rampart) + Phet (from Sanskrit vajra, diamond), meaning Wall of Diamonds, succeeding the 14th-century CE Sukhothai city of Chakangrao.

b_thap_chumphon.first_mention_attestation: 9th–10th century CE Old Mon and Pali inscription on a terracotta kumbha stupa excavated at Thap Chumphon, Nakhon Sawan Province
b_thap_chumphon.etymology_analysis: Modern Thai toponym from Thap (army camp) + Chumphon (assembly) applied to a Dvaravati moated site north of Nakhon Sawan whose terracotta kumbha inscription is dated paleographically to the 9th–10th centuries CE, not definitively <= 867 CE.

b_lampang.first_mention_attestation: 1301 CE conquest of Nakhon Khelang by King Mangrai of Lan Na (earlier 7th–8th century CE dates in Camadevivamsa [15th c.] and Jinakalamali [1516] are late retrospective chronicles; contemporary Hariphunchai Old Mon epigraphy begins in the 12th–13th centuries CE)
b_lampang.etymology_analysis: From Northern Thai Lam + pang (camp/clearing), the later name of Nakhon Khelang. Although 15th–16th century CE chronicles attribute Khelang's founding to the 7th–8th centuries CE, contemporary Hariphunchai epigraphy dates only to the 12th–13th centuries CE.

b_phayao.first_mention_attestation: 1096 CE founding of the Phayao Kingdom (Phu Kam Yao) in regional Northern Thai chronicles, flourishing in the 13th century CE
b_phayao.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Northern Thai Phu Kam Yao, referring to the 11th-century CE principality of Phayao. No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_phrae.first_mention_attestation: 1292 CE Ram Khamhaeng Inscription (Sukhothai Inscription No. 1) and 1336–1338 CE Wat Phra That Cho Hae foundation; the 828 CE date in local Tamnan legends is a late retrospective chronicle
b_phrae.etymology_analysis: Thai adaptation of Northern Thai Phae (spreading/raft). Contemporary epigraphic attestation begins with the 1292 CE Ram Khamhaeng Inscription; earlier 9th-century CE dates derive only from late Tamnan chronicles.

b_phetchabun.first_mention_attestation: Sukhothai-era (13th–14th century CE) frontier city on the Pa Sak River, distinct from the earlier Dvaravati site of Si Thep ~100 km to the south
b_phetchabun.etymology_analysis: From Thai Phetcha (Sanskrit vajra, diamond) + bun (Sanskrit pūrṇa, full), or reinterpreted from earlier Phuenchapura (city plenty of crops). Established in the Sukhothai era, post-867 CE.

b_phitsanulok.first_mention_attestation: 1357 CE foundation of Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat under King Lithai of Sukhothai (earlier known as Song Khwae in Sukhothai records; unified as Phitsanulok in the 15th century CE)
b_phitsanulok.etymology_analysis: From Thai Phitsanu (Sanskrit Viṣṇu) + lok (Sanskrit loka, world), meaning Realm of Vishnu, renamed from Song Khwae (Two Rivers) in the Sukhothai/Ayutthaya period. No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_phichit.first_mention_attestation: 1058 CE traditional founding of Sra Luang (later Okhaburi and Phichit) by Phraya Kotabongthevaraja
b_phichit.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit vicitra (beautiful, variegated), adopting the name Phichit after earlier names Sra Luang and Okhaburi. Post-867 CE foundation.

b_srideb.first_mention_attestation: 6th–7th century CE Sanskrit stone inscription K. 499, 7th–8th century CE śaṅkhalipi pillar inscription, and 8th-century CE clay sealings at Si Thep (Śrī Deva)
b_srideb.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Śrī Deva (auspicious deity), a major Dvaravati moated metropolis in the Pa Sak River valley contemporarily attested by 6th–8th century CE Sanskrit and śaṅkhalipi inscriptions and 4th–8th century CE archaeological remains.

b_sukhothai.first_mention_attestation: 1238 CE foundation of the Sukhothai Kingdom under Si Inthrathit, contemporarily attested in the 1292 CE Ram Khamhaeng Inscription (Sukhothai Inscription No. 1)
b_sukhothai.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Sukhodaya (sukha, happiness + udaya, rising/dawn), meaning Dawn of Happiness. No contemporary pre-867 CE epigraphic or chronicle attestation exists.

b_si_satchanalai.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1250 CE as the twin center of the Sukhothai Kingdom, contemporarily attested in the 1292 CE Ram Khamhaeng Inscription
b_si_satchanalai.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Śrī Sajjanālaya (auspicious abode of virtuous people), founded c. 1250 CE alongside Sukhothai. No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_sawangkaburi.first_mention_attestation: 1767–1770 CE Royal Chronicles of Ayutthaya and Thonburi recording Muang Sawangkaburi (modern Uttaradit area) during the Phra Fang faction uprising
b_sawangkaburi.etymology_analysis: From Thai Sawangka (Sanskrit svarga, heaven) + buri (Sanskrit purī, city), meaning Heavenly City. Attested only in late Ayutthaya/Thonburi-era records.

b_ban_lan.first_mention_attestation: Sukhothai-era (13th–14th century CE) western frontier patrol camp Ban Lan Khoi (modern Ban Dan Lan Hoi, Sukhothai Province)
b_ban_lan.etymology_analysis: From Thai Ban (village) + Lan (clearing/courtyard, from Sukhothai-era Ban Lan Khoi). No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_THAI_Phetchaburi.first_mention_attestation: 1191 CE Preah Khan inscription of Jayavarman VII naming Śrī Jayavajrapura (earlier 12th-century CE Phrip Phri; Yuan dynasty embassy in 1294 CE)
b_THAI_Phetchaburi.etymology_analysis: From Thai Phetcha (Sanskrit vajra, diamond) + buri (Sanskrit purī, city), meaning City of Diamonds, attested as Śrī Jayavajrapura in 1191 CE. No contemporary pre-867 CE attestation of the city name exists.

b_THAI_Chumpon.first_mention_attestation: 1098 CE historical record of Chumphon as a northern border city of Nakhon Si Thammarat
b_THAI_Chumpon.etymology_analysis: From Thai Chum (gather, assemble) + phon (troops/blessing, shortened from Chumnumphon), attested from 1098 CE as a frontier city of Nakhon Si Thammarat. No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_THAI_Singkhon.first_mention_attestation: 1760 CE Battle of Singkhon Pass during the Burmese–Siamese War (Alaungpaya's invasion of Ayutthaya via Tenasserim)
b_THAI_Singkhon.etymology_analysis: Named after Singkhon Pass (Dan Singkhon) in the Tenasserim Hills, an Ayutthaya-era border pass first prominently documented in 1760 CE. No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_THAI_Na_Rang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; Mueang Na Rang is documented only from the Ayutthaya period (1351–1767 CE) at the site of modern Prachuap Khiri Khan.
b_THAI_Na_Rang.etymology_analysis: Compound of the modern geographic prefix 'Thai' and Thai 'Na Rang' ('paddy field of the trough/channel'), referring to an Ayutthaya-period town (1351–1767 CE) at the site of Prachuap Khiri Khan. No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_THAI_Tenasserim.first_mention_attestation: 1383 CE Siamese city-pillar foundation record at Tanintharyi (Tenasserim); Khmer inscriptions from the wider Tenasserim area date only to the 12th–14th centuries CE.
b_THAI_Tenasserim.etymology_analysis: Combines the prefix 'Thai' with 'Tenasserim' (Burmese Tanintharyi, Thai Tanaosi), derived from Malay Tanah Seri ('glowing/splendid land') or Tanah Sirih ('betel land'). The town itself is first attested only in the late 14th century CE (1383 CE Siamese pillar), well after 867 CE.

b_THAI_Mergui.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; Mergui (Myeik) is attested as a port from the Pagan period (11th–13th centuries CE) and in 15th–16th century CE European and Ayutthaya accounts.

morphemes.translation: coastal port toponym of Mon-Burmese origin

b_THAI_Mergui.etymology_analysis: Combines the prefix 'Thai' with 'Mergui' (Burmese Myeik/Mrit, Mon Poik, Thai Marit), a peninsular port first documented in post-867 CE Pagan-era and 15th–16th century CE maritime records.

b_THAI_Kra_Buri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; Mueang Tra (Kra Buri) was established during the Ayutthaya Kingdom (1351–1767 CE) as a frontier town under Chumphon.
b_THAI_Kra_Buri.etymology_analysis: Combines the prefix 'Thai' with Thai 'Kra Buri' (from earlier Mueang Tra plus Sanskrit-derived 'buri', meaning city/town), an Ayutthaya-era (1351–1767 CE) frontier settlement with no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_thanbyuzayat.first_mention_attestation: 1874 CE, when a white tin-roofed rest-house (zayat) was built at the road junction by Mi Gee Yut, giving the settlement its name.
b_thanbyuzayat.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound meaning 'white-tin rest-house' (Mon Dung Jrop-bu), named after a tin-roofed travelers' pavilion erected in 1874 CE; entirely post-867 CE.

b_dawei.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; Dawei (Tavoy) is documented from the Pagan period (11th–13th centuries CE), while nearby Thagara yields artefacts spanning c. 9th–17th centuries CE.
b_dawei.etymology_analysis: Burmese Dawei (earlier English Tavoy) derives from Mon 'hawai' ('to sit cross-legged'). Although nearby Thagara has c. 9th–17th century CE archaeological remains, Dawei itself lacks contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation.

b_ye.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; Ye (Mon Dung Rew) is documented only as a post-Pagan Mon coastal town.

morphemes.form: Ye / Rew (ရေး / ရေဝ်)

b_ye.etymology_analysis: Burmese Ye (Mon Dung Rew) is a Mon coastal town at the mouth of the Ye River; no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE is known.

b_ramu.first_mention_attestation: 1437 CE in historical records of the Mrauk U Kingdom's expansion into the Chittagong–Ramu littoral (later also mentioned in the Rajmala and Alamgirnama).

morphemes.translation: regional settlement toponym associated with Rammabhumi

b_ramu.etymology_analysis: Toponym in southeastern Bangladesh (Cox's Bazar) associated with historical Rammabhumi/Ramvu; first clearly attested in 15th-century CE (1437 CE) Arakanese expansion accounts, with no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation of the town.

b_dianga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; attested in 16th-century CE Portuguese accounts as a trading settlement on the Karnaphuli River opposite Chittagong (prior to the 1607 CE massacre).
b_dianga.etymology_analysis: Name of a 16th–17th century CE Portuguese and Arakanese-era port settlement on the southern bank of the Karnaphuli River near Chittagong; entirely unattested by 867 CE.

b_sandoway.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; Thandwe (Thandaway/Sandoway) is first epigraphically attested in a 15th-century CE stone inscription from Parein (c. 1433–1459 CE) and in the 1437 CE Mrauk U conquest.
b_sandoway.etymology_analysis: Anglicized 'Sandoway' from Arakanese Thandway / Burmese Thandwe ('iron-bound' in folk etymology). Its classical Pali appellation Dvaravati is a later literary attribution, and contemporary epigraphic attestation of Thandaway begins only in the 15th century CE.

b_ramree.first_mention_attestation: 1327 CE in Arakanese historical records of a Pinya Kingdom raid on Ramree Island (and in 16th-century CE Portuguese accounts as Ramri).
b_ramree.etymology_analysis: Derived from classical Pali/Sanskrit Rammavati ('pleasant region') via the shortened local form Ram Pri Myo, rendered by Portuguese mariners as Ramri and anglicized as Ramree. Unattested before 1327 CE.

b_an.first_mention_attestation: 1334 CE (1333–1335 CE), when founded by King Min Hti of Launggyet as a pass stopover below the Arakan Mountains.
b_an.etymology_analysis: Arakanese/Burmese toponym for the strategic pass town founded in 1333–1335 CE by King Min Hti of Launggyet on the route across the Arakan Mountains; post-867 CE.

b_thabeik_taung.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; known only as a modern village tract in Buthidaung Township, northern Rakhine State.
b_thabeik_taung.etymology_analysis: Burmese descriptive compound meaning 'alms-bowl hill' (thabeik + taung), referring to a modern village tract in Buthidaung Township with no historical attestation by 867 CE.

b_matamuhuri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a settlement or administrative unit in contemporary records by 867 CE; a river name (Marma Mamuri) in southeastern Bangladesh.
b_matamuhuri.etymology_analysis: Directly adopts the proper hydronym of the Matamuhuri River (Bengali adaptation of Marma 'Mamuri') in southeastern Bangladesh; unattested as a settlement or polity by 867 CE.

b_vaisali.first_mention_attestation: 729 CE Sanskrit Anandachandra stone inscription from Vesali (now at Shitthaung Temple, Mrauk U), corroborated by 5th–8th century CE Candra dynasty coins and inscriptions.

morphemes.translation: spacious or broad city (named after Indian Vaishali)

b_vaisali.etymology_analysis: Pali/Prakrit Vesali (Burmese Waithali), named after the ancient Indian city of Vaishali. Contemporarily attested <= 867 CE as the capital of the Arakanese Candra kingdom via the 729 CE Anandachandra inscription and Candra coinage.

b_launggyet.first_mention_attestation: 1251 CE traditional founding of the Launggyet dynasty in the Arakanese chronicle Rakhine Razawin Thit (capital of Arakan 1251–1406 CE).
b_launggyet.etymology_analysis: Arakanese toponym for the final Le-Mro period capital of Arakan (1251–1406 CE), founded in 1251 CE and thus post-867 CE.

b_mrauk_u.first_mention_attestation: 1430 CE, when founded by King Min Saw Mon as the capital of the Kingdom of Mrauk U.
b_mrauk_u.etymology_analysis: Arakanese toponym (popularly glossed as 'monkey egg'), founded in 1430 CE by King Min Saw Mon as the capital of the Mrauk U Kingdom; post-867 CE.

b_mahamuni.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the toponym Mahamuni in contemporary records by 867 CE; the Mahamuni Buddha shrine at Dhanyawadi is attested from Pagan-era tradition (11th century CE) and 14th–15th century CE Arakanese sources.
b_mahamuni.etymology_analysis: Pali/Sanskrit compound Mahamuni ('Great Sage'), referring to the famed Buddha image and shrine near ancient Dhanyawadi; while Dhanyawadi appears in the 729 CE Anandachandra inscription, the toponym Mahamuni itself is not contemporarily attested <= 867 CE.

b_akyab.first_mention_attestation: 1825 CE during the First Anglo-Burmese War, when British forces occupied the fishing village and established the colonial port of Akyab (modern Sittwe) in 1826 CE.
b_akyab.etymology_analysis: Colonial English Akyab derives from Burmese/Arakanese Akyat-daw (Ahkyaib-daw), the name of a local relic stupa hill; developed into a formal town and port only in 1825–1826 CE.

b_hsenwi.first_mention_attestation: 1404 CE in Ming dynasty imperial records (seal of the Mubang Military and Civilian Pacification Commissioner); earlier 6th–7th century CE Siviraṭṭha dates come only from late Tai Yai chronicle legends.
b_hsenwi.etymology_analysis: Shan Hsenwi (Burmese Theinni, Chinese Mubang); late Tai Yai chronicles claim a legendary 6th–7th century CE origin (Siviraṭṭha), but contemporary attestation begins only in Ming dynasty records of 1404 CE.

b_monghsu.first_mention_attestation: 1857 CE, when Möng Hsu became an autonomous Shan state separated from Hsenwi in personal union with Möng Sang.
b_monghsu.etymology_analysis: Shan compound with 'möng' ('country/state/valley-town'); established as a distinct Shan polity only in 1857 CE, with no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_hsipaw.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; first contemporarily attested in a late 13th to early 14th century CE Burmese inscription of King Thihathu (c. 1265–1324 CE) mentioning Onbaung (Hsipaw).
b_hsipaw.etymology_analysis: Shan Hsipaw (Burmese Thibaw), earlier known as Onbaung. Local tradition claims a legendary 58 BCE Duṭṭhavatī origin, but contemporary epigraphic attestation begins only around the turn of the 14th century CE.

b_mongmit.first_mention_attestation: c. 1238 CE traditional founding of Möng Mit (later attested as a district of Hsenwi in 1413 CE and in King Bayinnaung's 1557 CE Shwezigon bell inscription).
b_mongmit.etymology_analysis: Shan compound with 'möng' ('country/state/valley-town'), burmanized as Momeik; founded c. 1238 CE and epigraphically attested in 1557 CE, well after 867 CE.

b_mongnai.first_mention_attestation: 1223 CE in Shan historical accounts (1318 CE in Northern Thai chronicles; contemporarily attested in 1556–1557 CE Toungoo campaigns).
b_mongnai.etymology_analysis: Shan compound with 'möng' ('country/state/valley-town'), burmanized as Mone; attributed to 1223 CE or 1318 CE in regional histories and contemporarily attested in 16th-century CE Toungoo records.

b_mongnawn.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary records by 867 CE; documented only as a 19th-century CE Shan sub-state separated from Hsenwi.
b_mongnawn.etymology_analysis: Shan compound meaning 'town/state by a lake' (burmanized as Maing Naung), using the generic topographic noun 'nawng' ('lake') rather than a proper hydronym; unattested by 867 CE.

b_mawkmai.first_mention_attestation: 1767 CE, when Mawkmai State was founded by Hsai Khiao.
b_mawkmai.etymology_analysis: Shan compound meaning 'new flower' (burmanized as Maukme), founded as a Shan state in 1767 CE; entirely post-867 CE.

b_nyaungshwe.first_mention_attestation: 1359 CE traditional founding of Yawnghwe (Nyaungshwe) in Shan and Burmese chronicles.
b_nyaungshwe.etymology_analysis: Burmese phonetic and folk-etymological adaptation of Shan Yawnghwe, the capital of Yawnghwe State founded in 1359 CE; post-867 CE.

b_taunggyi_south.first_mention_attestation: 1894 CE, when the British colonial administration established Taunggyi as the capital of the Southern Shan States (with 'South' as a modern directional qualifier).
b_taunggyi_south.etymology_analysis: Combines Burmese Taunggyi ('big mountain') with the English directional qualifier 'South'; Taunggyi itself was established as a colonial administrative town in 1894 CE, long after 867 CE.

b_laikha.first_mention_attestation: 1505 CE, when Laihka State was founded as a subordinate state under Hsenwi.
b_laikha.etymology_analysis: Shan toponym (burmanized as Legya/Lecha) for the Southern Shan state founded in 1505 CE; entirely post-867 CE.

b_mongkung.first_mention_attestation: 1835 CE, when Möng Küng was established as an autonomous Shan state (formerly a feudatory of Hsenwi).
b_mongkung.etymology_analysis: Shan compound with 'möng' ('country/state/valley-town'), burmanized as Maingkaing; established as an autonomous state in 1835 CE, with no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_ava.first_mention_attestation: Founded in September 1364 CE by King Thado Minbya at the confluence of the Irrawaddy and Myitnge rivers (site previously scouted in 1310 CE by Thihathu).
b_ava.etymology_analysis: English 'Ava' is a colonial/European corruption of Burmese Inwa (အင်းဝ), meaning 'entrance to the lake', referring to the site's position at the mouth of the lakes in the Kyaukse basin at the Irrawaddy-Myitnge confluence. Founded in 1364 CE, long after the 867 CE baseline.

b_pinya.first_mention_attestation: Founded on 7 February 1313 CE by King Thihathu as Wizayapura (Pali: Vijayapura), capital of the Pinya Kingdom.

morphemes.translation: Pinya (vernacular toponym of Vijayapura, 'City of Victory')

b_pinya.etymology_analysis: Pinya (Burmese: ပင်းယ), classically styled Wizayapura from Pali Vijayapura ('City of Victory'), was established in 1313 CE by Thihathu as the de jure successor capital to Bagan. It has no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_taungbyon.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bagan-period royal donation inscriptions (11th–13th centuries CE) and associated with King Anawrahta's reign (1044–1077 CE); no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_taungbyon.etymology_analysis: Older Burmese Tonplon (တောင်ပြုံး) means 'eroded mound'. Taungbyon served as a Bagan-era riverine fort and royal domain along the Irrawaddy north of Mandalay, attested from the Bagan period (11th–13th centuries CE) onward, post-dating 867 CE.

b_minbu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bagan-period epigraphy, including a 1278/1279 CE inscription recording Shin Ditha Pamauk's 1276–1277 CE mission to the Minbu region; no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation of the toponym.
b_minbu.etymology_analysis: Burmese Minbu (မင်းဘူး) is a vernacular toponym composed of min ('lord / king') and bu ('gourd / calabash'). While Pyu-era silver coins have been excavated in the broader Minbu basin, the settlement name Minbu is attested only from the Bagan period (11th–13th centuries CE), post-dating 867 CE.

b_salin.first_mention_attestation: Town founded in 1179 CE during the Bagan period; no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_salin.etymology_analysis: Salin (Burmese: စလင်း) is a historic town on the western bank of the Irrawaddy in the Minbu irrigated zone, founded in 1179 CE during the Bagan Dynasty and later a prominent noble appanage. It post-dates the 867 CE baseline.

b_ngape.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in later Burmese chronicles in connection with King Anawrahta's 11th-century CE march over the Ngape–An pass into Arakan; unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE sources.
b_ngape.etymology_analysis: Ngape (Burmese: ငဖဲ) is a town in Minbu District at the eastern foot of the Arakan Yoma pass to An. Its earliest historical associations date to the 11th-century CE Bagan period in Burmese chronicles, with no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_shwesettaw.first_mention_attestation: Historical pilgrimage site relocated and documented under King Thalun in 1638 CE (though local Buddhist tradition claims earlier worship); unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE records.
b_shwesettaw.etymology_analysis: Burmese Shwesettaw (ရွှေစက်တော်) literally means 'Golden Sacred Footprint', referring to the two supposed footprints of Gautama Buddha at Mann Shwesettaw in Minbu. Documented historically from the Toungoo/Konbaung periods (1638 CE), well after 867 CE.

b_pagan.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary external record is a Song dynasty tribute mission from Pugan (Bagan) in 1004/1005 CE (Zhufanzhi), followed by the 1050 CE Cham inscription (Pukam); late chronicles claim 849 CE fortification, but radiocarbon dating of the walls points to c. 980–1020 CE.

morphemes.form: pukam / pugan (ပုဂန် / ပုဂံ)

b_pagan.etymology_analysis: Modern Bagan derives from Burmese Pugan (ပုဂံ) and Old Burmese Pukam (ပုဂန်), classically styled Arimaddanapura ('City that Tramples on Enemies') in Pali. While 18th–19th century chronicles claim King Pyinbya fortified it in 849 CE, no contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation exists; radiocarbon dates for Old Bagan walls are c. 980–1020 CE and the earliest contemporary written records date to 1004/1005 CE.

b_popa.first_mention_attestation: Associated with the Bagan Kingdom from the 11th century CE onward (e.g., King Anawrahta's rebellion at Mount Popa in 1044 CE and nat shrines); no contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation.
b_popa.etymology_analysis: Popa (Burmese: ပုပ္ပား, from Pali puppha / Sanskrit puṣpa meaning 'flower') directly adopts the name of the sacred dormant volcano Mount Popa (Popa Taung) in central Myanmar. It is attested in Bagan-era history from the 11th century CE, with no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_myitche.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE records; modern river town in Pakokku Township on the west bank of the Irrawaddy.
b_myitche.etymology_analysis: Burmese Myitche / Myit Chay (မြစ်ခြေ) combines myit ('river') and chay ('foot / base'), referring to its location on the lower bank of the Irrawaddy in Pakokku Township. There is no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_tantkyitaung.first_mention_attestation: Tantkyitaung Pagoda on Tantkyi Hill is traditionally dated to 397 ME (1035 CE) under King Anawrahta; no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_tantkyitaung.etymology_analysis: Tantkyitaung (တန့်ကြည့်တောင်) is the Burmese name of Tantkyi Hill across the Irrawaddy from Bagan, literally 'pause-and-look mountain'. Its pagoda is dated to 1035 CE in Burmese tradition, post-dating 867 CE.

b_nyaung_u.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Bagan period (Shwezigon Pagoda completed 1102 CE in Nyaung-U, and associated with 10th-century ruler Nyaung-u Sawrahan); no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_nyaung_u.etymology_analysis: Burmese Nyaung-U (ညောင်ဦး) combines nyaung ('banyan tree') and u ('head / upstream end'), denoting the northern settlement of the Bagan zone. First attested in the Bagan period (10th–12th centuries CE), post-dating 867 CE.

b_powundaung.first_mention_attestation: Phowintaung Buddhist cave complex has statues and murals dated from the 14th to 18th centuries CE; no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_powundaung.etymology_analysis: Powundaung / Phowintaung (ဖိုလ်ဝင်တောင်) directly names the sandstone mountain west of Monywa housing 14th–18th century CE Buddhist cave shrines ('Mountain of Isolated Solitary Meditation'). It post-dates the 867 CE baseline.

b_sagaing.first_mention_attestation: Established as a fortified capital in 1315 CE by Saw Yun (Athinkhaya) of the Sagaing Kingdom (classical Pali name Jayapura / Jeyyapura); no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_sagaing.etymology_analysis: Sagaing (Burmese: စစ်ကိုင်း, MLCTS: cac kuing:) derives from sit ('Albizia tree') and kaing ('branch / riverside grove'), with the classical Pali title Jayapura ('City of Victory'). Established as a kingdom capital in 1315 CE, well after 867 CE.

b_halin.first_mention_attestation: Contemporarily attested by Pyu stone inscriptions from Halin (c. 3rd–6th centuries CE; inscribed gate bricks 1st–3rd centuries CE) and Tang Chinese chronicles (Man Shu 863 CE, Xin Tangshu) recording the 832 CE Nanzhao raid on Halin.
b_halin.etymology_analysis: Halin (also Hanlin or Halingyi; ဟန်လင်း) was one of the three major walled Pyu city-states in Upper Myanmar's Mu valley, occupied from the 2nd century BCE to c. 870 CE. Contemporarily attested <= 867 CE via early Pyu epigraphy (c. 3rd–6th centuries CE) and Tang Chinese chronicles recording the 832 CE Nanzhao sack.

b_myinmu.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Burmese chronicle tradition from the 11th century CE (home of Anawrahta's paladin Nga Htwe Yu); unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE sources.
b_myinmu.etymology_analysis: Myinmu (Burmese: မြင်းမူ) is a river town on the northern bank of the Irrawaddy near the mouth of the Mu River in Sagaing Region. While prehistoric/Pyu settlements exist in the surrounding township, the toponym Myinmu has no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_yamethin.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a Bagan/Pinya-era frontier town (raided by Toungoo in 1358–1359 CE and prominent in 14th–15th century CE Ava records); late chronicles claim an earlier foundation as Nwamethin, but there is no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

morphemes.form: nwa-me / yame (နွားမည်း / ရမည်း)

b_yamethin.etymology_analysis: Yamethin (Burmese: ရမည်းသင်း) evolved from earlier Nwamethin (နွားမည်းသင်း, 'herd of black cows') via Namethin. It is documented historically from the late Bagan/Pinya period (14th century CE), post-dating 867 CE.

b_peikthanomyo.first_mention_attestation: The Pyu walled site of Beikthano is radiocarbon dated c. 200 BCE–610 CE with a 2nd–4th century CE Prakrit/Brahmi clay seal (Samghasiri), but the Burmese name Beikthano Myo / Peikthanomyo ('Vishnu City') is a modern scholarly designation not attested in contemporary <= 867 CE records.
b_peikthanomyo.etymology_analysis: Peikthanomyo (Beikthano Myo, ဗိဿနိုးမြို့) means 'Vishnu City'. Although the underlying archaeological ruins are one of the oldest Pyu urban centers (c. 200 BCE–610 CE), Michael Aung-Thwin notes that the toponym Beikthano is not attested in contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphy or early chronicles, being applied retroactively.

b_binnaka.first_mention_attestation: Pyu-era archaeological site with Pyu-script terracotta tablets and silver coins, but the toponym Binnaka is attested only in late Burmese chronicles (Hmannan Yazawin, 1829 CE) and a 19th-century Konbaung sittan; no contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation.
b_binnaka.etymology_analysis: Binnaka is an ancient walled site in central Myanmar yielding Pyu, Pagan, Ava, and Konbaung artifacts. However, the name Binnaka itself is absent from contemporary <= 867 CE inscriptions and external chronicles, appearing only in late Burmese chronicles and Konbaung records.

b_dagon.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Dagon in the early 11th century CE (c. 1028–1043 CE) by the Mon, and epigraphically attested as dgun / Dagon in 15th-century Mon inscriptions (Kalyani 1479 CE, Shwedagon 1485 CE); no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: Dagon (felled tree / log poised horizontally; traditional Mon etymology)

b_dagon.etymology_analysis: Dagon (Burmese: ဒဂုံ, Old Mon: dgun) was a Mon settlement around the Shwedagon hill before King Alaungpaya renamed it Yangon in 1755 CE. Founded in the early 11th century CE and attested in 15th-century Mon epigraphy, it post-dates 867 CE.

b_syriam.first_mention_attestation: Prominent in late 16th-century CE Portuguese and Burmese records (seized by Filipe de Brito in 1599 CE); unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE sources.

morphemes.form: sreang / tanyin (သြေၚ် / သန်လျင်)
morphemes.translation: Thanlyin (corrupted in European sources as Syriam)

b_syriam.etymology_analysis: Syriam is the European/colonial rendering of Burmese Thanlyin (သန်လျင်, pronounced Tanyin), derived from Mon Sreang (သြေၚ်). It rose to prominence as a major Lower Myanmar port in the 16th–18th centuries CE, with no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

b_krapan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Krapan (Middle Mon Kraban / Burmese Khabin) in a 1198 CE Old Burmese stone inscription from the reign of King Narapatisithu (discussed in G. H. Luce's epigraphic studies and Michael Aung-Thwin, The Mists of Rāmañña); no <= 867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: unattested toponym in the Dagon / Lower Myanmar delta

b_krapan.etymology_analysis: From Middle Mon Kraban / Old Burmese Krapan (later Khabin), a Lower Burma settlement first attested in a 1198 CE Pagan-period inscription (post-867 CE).

b_bogale.first_mention_attestation: Named in the early 19th century CE as Bogaleseik ('Little Foreigner Port') after the hunting camp of Anglo-Burmese hunter U Maung Kalay; unattested <= 867 CE.
b_bogale.eponym_details: Named after Bo Kalay ('little foreigner/European'), an early 19th-century Anglo-Burmese hunter (U Maung Kalay) whose hunting camp in the Irrawaddy Delta became Bogaleseik ('Little Foreigner Port').
b_bogale.etymology_analysis: Bogale (Burmese: ဘိုကလေး, shortened from Bogaleseik ဘိုကလေးဆိပ် 'Little Foreigner Port') originated in the early 19th century CE from the camp of Anglo-Burmese hunter U Maung Kalay (Bo Kalay). It is both post-867 and named after a post-867 person.

b_kusumi.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Kusima in a 1165 CE Sri Lankan rock inscription (reign of Parakramabahu I), and in Burmese records from 1265 CE; no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: Kusima (classical Pali name of Pathein / Bassein)

b_kusumi.etymology_analysis: Kusumi (Pali: Kusima) is the classical Pali name of Pathein (Bassein, from Old Mon pha-sɛm 'big sea'). First contemporarily attested in a 1165 CE Sri Lankan rock inscription, three centuries after 867 CE.

b_myaungmya.first_mention_attestation: Earliest referenced in the Jambudipa text dating to the reign of King Kyansittha (r. 1084–1112 CE), and prominent as a fortified delta city in 1364–1390 CE; no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_myaungmya.etymology_analysis: Burmese Myaungmya (မြောင်းမြ) derives from Mon Mongmale (မံၚ်မၠ), meaning 'where the Myaya plants are'. Attested from the late 11th–14th centuries CE, post-dating 867 CE.

b_negrais.first_mention_attestation: Documented in the 16th century CE (Taungoo–Mrauk-U War 1545–1547 CE and Portuguese maritime charts as Negrais); no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_negrais.etymology_analysis: Negrais is the Portuguese borrowing of Burmese Nagarit (နဂရစ်), from Sanskrit nāgarāja ('dragon king'), referring to Cape Negrais (Mawtin Point) at the southwestern tip of Myanmar. Attested in 16th-century CE maritime and war records, post-dating 867 CE.

b_sittaung.first_mention_attestation: Walled town of Sittaung is attested as one of the 32 myo (towns) of the 16th-century CE Hanthawaddy Kingdom; no contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: Sittaung (river and walled town near its mouth)

b_sittaung.etymology_analysis: Sittaung (Burmese: စစ်တောင်း) directly adopts the hydronym of the Sittaung River, located beside the historical walled town of Sittaung in Mon State. While pre-Bagan artifacts exist near nearby Kyaikkatha, the toponym Sittaung is attested in historical records from the Hanthawaddy period (16th century CE), post-dating 867 CE.

b_shwegyin.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 19th century CE (site of the founding of the Shwegyin Nikaya Buddhist order in 1860 CE); no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_shwegyin.etymology_analysis: Burmese Shwegyin (ရွှေကျင်) means 'gold-panning' (from shwe 'gold' + kyin 'to pan/sift'), reflecting local alluvial gold deposits along the Shwegyin River. Attested in the modern/Konbaung era, well after 867 CE.

b_thaton.first_mention_attestation: Earliest dated nearby inscriptions are the 1098 CE Kyaik Talan and Kyaik Te inscriptions of Kyanzittha; the toponym Sudhuim/Sudhammapura (Thaton) appears in Pagan/Ava and 1486 CE Mon inscriptions (the 1067 CE Manuho inscription is a late 16th-century forgery); no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.

morphemes.translation: city of Sudhamma (the assembly hall of the gods)

b_thaton.etymology_analysis: Burmese Thaton (သထုံ) derives from Mon Sadhuim / Sudhuim (သဓီု), itself from Pali Sudhammapura ('City of Sudhamma'). Although Mon tradition claims an ancient Suvannabhumi kingdom from the 6th century BCE, scholarship (including Michael Aung-Thwin) finds no contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic attestation of Thaton.

b_muttina.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary evidence is a 1176 CE stone inscription erected by King Sithu II of the Bagan Empire; no contemporary <= 867 CE attestation.
b_muttina.etymology_analysis: Muttina (a variant of Muttama / Mottama, historically Martaban) derives from Mon Mumaw (မုဟ်တၟံ, /mùh mɔˀ/), meaning 'rocky spur'. First contemporarily attested in a 1176 CE Bagan inscription of Sithu II, post-dating 867 CE.

b_mawlamyine.first_mention_attestation: 1479 CE Kalyani Stone Inscriptions of King Dhammazedi of Hanthawaddy Pegu (listing Mawlamyine among the 32 regional cities of Martaban)
b_mawlamyine.etymology_analysis: Burmese adaptation of Mon Mot-mua-lum (Moulmein), meaning 'damaged eye' or 'one-eyed', associated with a Mon royal legend. First contemporarily attested in the 1479 CE Kalyani Stone Inscriptions.

b_taikkala.first_mention_attestation: 1479 CE Kalyani Stone Inscription of King Dhammazedi (recording Golamattikanagara / Taikkala; earlier Mon occupation at Ayetthema lacks contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic naming)
b_taikkala.etymology_analysis: Mon/Burmese rendering of Pali Golamattikanagara ('mud-brick city of the Gola people'). Although 1479 CE Kalyani inscriptions retroactively link it to Ashoka's 3rd-century BCE mission to Suvannabhumi, no contemporary <= 867 CE written attestation of the toponym exists.

b_hinthada.first_mention_attestation: c. 1755 CE Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War records (first historically mentioned during King Alaungpaya's conquest of Lower Burma)
b_hinthada.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Mon name Henzada for the abundant local danone palm (with a Burmese folk etymology linking it to hintha, 'Brahminy duck/sheldrake'). First historically attested in the mid-18th century CE.

b_myanaung.first_mention_attestation: 1754 CE Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War records (renamed Myanaung by King Alaungpaya after a naval victory; predecessor Mon settlement Gu Htut dates to c. 1250 CE)
b_myanaung.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound meaning 'succeed quickly', bestowed by King Alaungpaya in 1754 CE on the earlier Mon settlement of Gu Htut (founded c. 1250 CE).

b_magwe.first_mention_attestation: Early 15th-century CE Ava-Pegu War historical records (listing Magwe among Irrawaddy riverine towns alongside Sagu and Salin)
b_magwe.etymology_analysis: Burmese toponym traditionally interpreted as 'not separated' (or linked in local tradition to Pali maghava). Unattested before the post-Pagan Ava period (c. 15th century CE).

b_shwemyo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-modern historical records <= 867 CE; modern village in Tatkon Township, Naypyidaw Union Territory
b_shwemyo.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound meaning 'golden town'. Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE sources and unoccupied in the repository.

b_sriksetra.first_mention_attestation: 5th-6th century CE Khin Ba Mound golden Pali/Pyu inscriptions and Pyu Vikrama-dynasty urn inscriptions; also contemporarily attested by Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang in 648 CE
b_sriksetra.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit toponym meaning 'auspicious field' (Burmese Thayekhittaya). Major Pyu city-state contemporarily attested via 5th-6th century CE Pyu/Pali inscriptions and 7th-century CE Chinese Tang records (Xuanzang 648 CE, Yijing 675 CE).

b_myede.first_mention_attestation: Early 15th-century CE Ava-Hanthawaddy War records (attesting Myede on the eastern bank of the Irrawaddy; Aunglan was later established adjacent to it after 1852 CE)
b_myede.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound (Myayde) meaning 'inland earth/territory'. Attested only from the post-Pagan Ava period (c. 15th century CE), with no <= 867 CE record.

b_thayetmyo.first_mention_attestation: Early 15th-century CE Ava-Pegu War records (attesting Thayet on the western bank of the Irrawaddy opposite Myede)
b_thayetmyo.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound meaning 'mango town'. Attested in the Ava period (c. 15th century CE) and prominent later as a British frontier station; no <= 867 CE attestation exists.

b_taungdwingyi.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE Ava Kingdom campaign records (subjugated by King Thadominbya in 1365 CE)
b_taungdwingyi.etymology_analysis: Burmese toponym meaning 'great mountain-basin' (or 'great southern basin'). While the nearby Pyu site of Beikthano dates to the 1st-5th centuries CE, the town of Taungdwingyi itself is unattested before 1365 CE.

b_toungoo.first_mention_attestation: 1279 CE late Pagan period foundation (founded 17 April 1279 CE by Thawun Gyi; later independent under Mingyi Nyo in 1510 CE)
b_toungoo.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound (Taung-ngu) meaning 'hill spur', referring to its position in the narrow Sittaung valley. Founded in 1279 CE, over four centuries after 867 CE.

b_mong_pai.first_mention_attestation: 1542-1545 CE Ava-Toungoo period records (fief of Sao Hso Kaw Hpa / Mobye Narapati, son of Hkonmaing of Hsipaw)
b_mong_pai.etymology_analysis: Shan toponym (Burmese Mobye) composed of möng ('state/valley') and pai. Emerged as a Shan princely state in the post-Pagan period and is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_swa.first_mention_attestation: 1191 CE Pagan period administrative record (King Sithu II appointing Ananda Thuriya governor of Kanba Myint on the Swa stream)
b_swa.etymology_analysis: Named after Swa Creek (Swa Chaung), a tributary of the Sittaung River in Yedashe Township. The Swa stream valley is attested from 1191 CE under the Pagan Kingdom, with no <= 867 CE written record.

b_hanlan.first_mention_attestation: Contemporarily attested at Halin (Hanlin) by Pyu-script inscriptions (c. 3rd–6th centuries CE; inscribed gate bricks 1st–3rd centuries CE; TSK 6 funerary inscription naming Lord Ruba), followed by 8th–9th century CE Sri Trivikrama inscriptions and 832 CE Tang Chinese records.
b_hanlan.etymology_analysis: Ancient Pyu city-state (Halin / Hanlin) in Upper Myanmar, contemporarily attested by Pyu-script inscriptions from c. 300 CE onward (c. 3rd–6th centuries CE) and Tang Chinese accounts of the 832 CE Nanzhao raid.

b_maukkadaw.first_mention_attestation: 1901 CE Upper Chindwin District Gazetteer (colonial administrative record of Maukkadaw village on the Chindwin River)
b_maukkadaw.etymology_analysis: Burmese riverine toponym on the Chindwin River in Mingin Township. Unattested in <= 867 CE or Pagan-era sources.

b_mingiu.first_mention_attestation: 18th-century CE Konbaung Dynasty administrative records (Mingin jurisdiction on the right bank of the Chindwin River)
b_mingiu.etymology_analysis: Romanization variant of Mingin (Burmese မင်းကင်း), a Chindwin River town attested from the Konbaung period (18th century CE) with no <= 867 CE attestation.

b_kale.first_mention_attestation: Mid-11th century CE Mon-language votive tablet of King Anawrahta (r. 1044-1077 CE) unearthed at Kalay; traditional chronicles cite 966 CE

morphemes.translation: town surrounded by four satellite towns

b_kale.etymology_analysis: Derived from earlier Burmese Karlaymyo ('town surrounded by four satellite towns', later folk-etymologized as Kalaymyo, 'town of children'). Earliest contemporary material dates to the 11th-century CE Pagan period.

b_chin.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Pagan-period Old Burmese stone inscriptions (recording the ethnonym Khyan / Khyang in the Chindwin Valley)
b_chin.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym for the Chin (Zo) peoples of western Myanmar, evolved from Old Burmese Khyan/Khyang first attested in 11th-century CE Pagan inscriptions.

b_hsawnghsup.first_mention_attestation: 1470 CE Manipur chronicles (recording the joint conquest of Hsawnghsup/Somsok by King Kiyamba of Manipur and Pong)
b_hsawnghsup.etymology_analysis: Shan name (called Thaungdut in Burmese and Somsok in Manipuri) for an outlying Shan princely state in the Kabaw Valley, founded c. 15th century CE.

b_madaya.first_mention_attestation: 18th-century CE Konbaung-period records and Zambudipa Okhsaung Kyan (attesting Madaya north of Amarapura/Mandalay)
b_madaya.etymology_analysis: Burmese toponym (မတ္တရာ) for a town north of Mandalay. Documented in Konbaung-era administrative records and chronicles, with no <= 867 CE attestation.

b_momeik.first_mention_attestation: 1413 CE attestation as a district of Hsenwi (Möng Mit / Momeik), followed by 1542 CE Ava–Toungoo war records and King Bayinnaung's 1557 CE Shwezigon Pagoda bell inscription.
b_momeik.etymology_analysis: Burmese rendering of Shan Möng Mit, a northern Shan state on the Shweli River; attested from 1413 CE onward (post-867 CE).

b_singu.first_mention_attestation: 1300 CE Second Mongol invasion of Burma records (Myinsaing forces attacking the Mongol garrison at Nga Singu)
b_singu.etymology_analysis: Burmese toponym (Singu / Nga Singu) north of Mandalay, first contemporarily attested in 1300 CE during the Myinsaing-Yuan conflict.

b_takon.first_mention_attestation: Mid-11th century CE Pagan-period votive tablets of King Anawrahta and 12th-century CE Bagan stone inscriptions (later Yuanshi records Tagaung in 1284 CE; Hmannan Yazawin's 850 BCE claim is a late 1832 CE legend)
b_takon.etymology_analysis: Old Burmese spelling (Takôn / Tagaung) of the Upper Irrawaddy riverine town. While archaeology shows Pyu-era habitation, the toponym itself has no contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic or Tang-era attestation, first appearing in 11th-12th century CE Pagan records.

b_wuntho.first_mention_attestation: 1555 CE Toungoo conquest records (mentioning the governor of Wuntho, nephew of the Möng Yang saopha)
b_wuntho.etymology_analysis: Burmese adaptation of Shan Wying Hsö ('city of the tiger'). First attested historically in 1555 CE during Bayinnaung's Upper Burma campaign.

b_htigyaing.first_mention_attestation: 1277 CE First Mongol invasion of Burma records (Yuan forces turning back at Htigyaing before capturing it in 1283 CE)
b_htigyaing.etymology_analysis: Burmese river-port toponym on the upper Irrawaddy. First attested in 1277 CE during the Mongol-Yuan campaigns against the Pagan Kingdom.

b_myedu.first_mention_attestation: 1413 CE Ava-Maw Shan conflict records (Prince Minye Kyawswa defeating Maw forces at Myedu in the Mu valley)
b_myedu.etymology_analysis: Burmese toponym in the Mu River valley (Kanbalu Township). First attested in 15th-century CE Ava-period military records, with no <= 867 CE attestation.

b_momauk.first_mention_attestation: 1904 CE British colonial forestry and administrative records of Kachin State (Bhamo District)
b_momauk.etymology_analysis: Burmese rendering of Shan Möng Mok (Mauk), a borderland town near Bhamo in Kachin State. Unattested prior to the late pre-colonial/colonial era.

b_bumangdian.first_mention_attestation: Dali Kingdom period (937-1253 CE) administrative records (naming the Ruili/Dehong border area Bumangdian under Tengyue Prefecture)
b_bumangdian.etymology_analysis: Dali Kingdom-era Chinese/Tai administrative name (布茫甸) for the Dehong/Ruili valley, postdating 867 CE.

b_waingmaw.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-modern historical records <= 867 CE; modern Kachin State town opposite Myitkyina
b_waingmaw.etymology_analysis: Shan compound meaning 'new town' (or 'new walled city'). Modern settlement across the Irrawaddy from Myitkyina with no <= 867 CE attestation.

b_monyin.first_mention_attestation: c. 13th-century CE Shan-state records (emergence of the Shan principality of Möng Yang / Mohnyin in northern Myanmar)
b_monyin.etymology_analysis: Burmese rendering (Mohnyin / Monyin) of Shan Möng Yang, a major northern Shan state that emerged in the 13th century CE (post-867 CE).

b_hpakant.first_mention_attestation: Established as a village in 1832 CE and re-established in 1836 CE after a landslide, per modern historical accounts of Hpakant jade mining.
b_hpakant.etymology_analysis: Borrowed into Burmese from Shan words meaning 'rock fall' or 'building up a wall.' First established as a settlement in 1832 CE, well after 867 CE.

b_mogaung.first_mention_attestation: First attested in contemporary Chinese Yuan dynasty records in 1295 CE as Mengguang (蒙光), when a Tribal Command was established there.
b_mogaung.etymology_analysis: Burmese Mogaung adapts the Shan state name Möng Kawng ('Land/City of the Drum'). Contemporary written attestation begins in 1295 CE in Yuan records, post-867 CE.

b_shwegu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic, numismatic, or external chronicle sources; known only from later Burmese administrative history.
b_shwegu.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound meaning 'golden cave.' No contemporary <= 867 CE attestation exists for the settlement.

b_myitkyina.first_mention_attestation: First attested in late 19th-century colonial and missionary records beginning around 1890 CE (with formal British administrative establishment in 1892-1895 CE).
b_myitkyina.etymology_analysis: Burmese locator compound meaning 'near the big river' (referring to the Irrawaddy). Attested only from the 1890s CE, post-867 CE.

b_danai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; documented only in modern Kachin and Burmese administrative records.
b_danai.etymology_analysis: Adapted into Burmese as Tanai/Danai from the Jingpo hydronym Tanai (Tanai Hka, the upper Chindwin River). No contemporary <= 867 CE settlement attestation exists.

b_sumpra_bum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; appears in 20th-century colonial and World War II records.
b_sumpra_bum.etymology_analysis: Jingpo descriptive topographic compound meaning 'jungle grass mountain.' Unattested by 867 CE.

b_nandian.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1289 CE (Zhiyuan 26, Yuan dynasty) when Nandian Lu (南甸路军民总管府) was established, as recorded in Ming-era Yunnan gazetteers.
b_nandian.etymology_analysis: Chinese directional-topographic name meaning 'southern basin.' First attested as an administrative unit in 1289 CE under the Yuan dynasty, post-867 CE.

b_nujiang_lisu.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1954 CE as the Nujiang Lisu Autonomous Region (renamed Autonomous Prefecture in 1957 CE).
b_nujiang_lisu.etymology_analysis: Modern 1954 CE administrative compound combining the Chinese name of the Salween River (Nujiang) with the Lisu ethnonym; post-867 CE.

b_chihpwi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; recorded only in modern Kachin and Burmese administrative records.
b_chihpwi.etymology_analysis: Likely derived from the Lacid (Lashi) word for 'beeswax,' adapted into Burmese as Chipwi/Chihpwi. Unattested by 867 CE.

b_sawlaw.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; recorded only in modern Kachin and Burmese administrative records.
b_sawlaw.etymology_analysis: Likely derived from Lhaovo words meaning 'hard to breathe,' adapted into Burmese as Hsawlaw/Sawlaw. Unattested by 867 CE.

b_kokang.first_mention_attestation: The polity was founded in 1739 CE as Xingdahu by Yang Shien-tsai and renamed Kokang (Guogan, 果敢) after 1795 CE by Yang Yougen, with Qing recognition in 1840 CE.
b_kokang.etymology_analysis: Derived from Shan Kao Kang ('nine guards/households') and sinicized as Guogan (果敢) in the late 18th to 19th century CE; post-867 CE.

b_putao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; the area was later known as the Shan state of Hkamti Long, with Fort Hertz built by the British in 1914 CE.
b_putao.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in northern Kachin State (historically centered in the Khamti Shan polity of Hkamti Long). Unattested by 867 CE.

b_nongmun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; documented only in modern Kachin and Burmese administrative records.
b_nongmun.etymology_analysis: Derived from Shan ၼွၵ်ႈမိူင်း meaning 'outside the country,' adapted into Burmese as Nogmung/Nongmun. Unattested by 867 CE.

b_hkawlanghu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; documented in 20th-century accounts (e.g., Reginald Farrer's burial there in 1920 CE).
b_hkawlanghu.etymology_analysis: Derived from Rawang words meaning 'Kawnglang's village.' Unattested in <= 867 CE contemporary records.

b_moeng_laem.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1289 CE when Möng Lem (Menglian) was established as a tusi state under the Yuan dynasty.
b_moeng_laem.etymology_analysis: Tai Nüa polity name Möng Lem (sinicized as Menglian 孟连), first attested as a Yuan-era tusi in 1289 CE, post-867 CE.

b_keng_tung.first_mention_attestation: Kengtung State is attested from 1243 CE (with late 13th-century Lanna/Tai Khün founding accounts in local chronicles).
b_keng_tung.etymology_analysis: Shan/Tai Khün compound Keng Tung ('walled city of Tung,' classical Pali Tungapuri). Attested from the 13th century CE (1243 CE), post-867 CE.

b_mong_yang.first_mention_attestation: Established as a Shan state around the late 13th to early 14th century CE (c. 1300 CE), appearing in Yuan and Ming Chinese records as Mengyang (孟养).
b_mong_yang.etymology_analysis: Shan state name Möng Yang (Burmese Mohnyin, Chinese Mengyang 孟养). First attested around the late 13th century CE, post-867 CE.

b_asian_wa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE written sources; 'Asian Wa' is a modern ethnonymic label and the local 'Jingmadian' designation is unattested by 867 CE.
b_asian_wa.etymology_analysis: Modern English-Wa ethnonymic designation for the Wa people of the Yunnan-Myanmar borderlands; unattested as a polity or settlement by 867 CE.

b_gengma.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the early Ming dynasty Hongwu era (1368-1398 CE) following 14th-century Tai migration from Möng Mao.
b_gengma.etymology_analysis: Sinicization (耿马) of the Tai name meaning 'city of the white horse.' Attested from the early Ming period (late 14th century CE), post-867 CE.

b_lincang.first_mention_attestation: Named Lincang in 1954 CE (previously known as Mianning / Mengmian in the Ming-Qing periods); unattested as a settlement in <= 867 CE records.
b_lincang.etymology_analysis: Chinese directional compound meaning 'facing the Lancang (Mekong) River,' coined in 1954 CE; post-867 CE.

b_yongchang_yongchang.first_mention_attestation: Contemporarily attested in 69 CE (Yongping 12, Eastern Han) when Yongchang Commandery (永昌郡) was established, recorded in Dongguan Hanji and Book of the Later Han.
b_yongchang_yongchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Han-era Chinese administrative name meaning 'eternal prosperity,' established in 69 CE as Yongchang Commandery in modern Baoshan, Yunnan.

b_yongchang_shengxiang.first_mention_attestation: Yuan Shi (ch. 61) records its 1274 CE Yuan-era reorganization as Yongping County (under Yongchang), while retrospectively attributing Shengxiang Commandery (勝鄉郡) to the Tang-era Nanzhao Meng clan (c. 794 CE).
b_yongchang_shengxiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name ('superior/victorious district'). Although Yuan Shi (1370 CE) attributes Shengxiang Commandery to Nanzhao in the Tang period, no contemporary <= 867 CE text attests the name Shengxiang; the same site was contemporarily attested as Bonan County (博南縣) in 69 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu) / Dongguan Hanji (69 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Eastern Han established Bonan County (博南縣) in 69 CE under Yongchang Commandery; Nanzhao later renamed it Shengxiang Commandery.

b_yongchang_qingdian.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1327 CE (Taiding 4, Yuan dynasty) when Qingdian County (慶甸縣) was established alongside Shunning Prefecture, recorded in Yuan Shi and Xin Yuan Shi.
b_yongchang_qingdian.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name ('auspicious basin') for the Yuan-era county in modern Fengqing County, Yunnan; first attested in 1327 CE, post-867 CE.

b_pegu.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary external mention dates to a 1195 CE Chinese source noting Jayavarman VII's claim over Pegu, with the earliest extant Burmese epigraphic mentions in 1212 CE and 1266 CE (earlier 573/825 CE dates come only from late Mon chronicles).
b_pegu.etymology_analysis: Burmese Pè-khu / English Pegu derives from the Mon toponym Bago. Despite late chronicle legends claiming 6th-9th century CE origins, contemporary evidence begins in 1195-1212 CE, post-867 CE.

b_tharrawaddy.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1574 CE when Toungoo prince Min Tha Sit (later Nawrahta Minsaw) was appointed governor of Tharrawaddy.
b_tharrawaddy.etymology_analysis: Burmese adaptation of Pali Sārāvatī ('possessing essence/excellence'). Attested from the 16th century CE (1574 CE), predating King Tharrawaddy Min (who was named after the town); post-867 CE.

b_phyu.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the late 13th to early 14th century CE (c. 1300 CE) in Hanthawaddy Kingdom documents as a settlement conquered from the Pyu.
b_phyu.etymology_analysis: Named after the Pyu people, though the modern town of Phyu itself is first documented in Hanthawaddy-era records around 1300 CE, post-867 CE.

b_kyaukse.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 12th-13th century CE Pagan-period stone inscriptions (c. 1100 CE), which refer to the irrigated Kyaukse basin as 'the first home.'
b_kyaukse.etymology_analysis: Burmese compound meaning 'stone weir,' referring to its ancient irrigation works. Although Burman settlement likely began around 800 CE, contemporary written attestation begins in 12th-century CE inscriptions, post-867 CE.

b_maingmaw.first_mention_attestation: The Shan-derived name Maingmaw (Möng Mao) applied to the Pyu walled site of Pinle is unattested in contemporary <= 867 CE sources; the underlying Pyu urban site (c. 200–900 CE) is attested archaeologically through city walls, silver coinage, and Pyu-script inscriptions.
b_maingmaw.etymology_analysis: The post-867 CE name Maingmaw adapts Shan Möng Mao, applied to the 1st-millennium CE Pyu walled urban center (also called Pinle) in the Kyaukse plain; while the underlying Pyu site is archaeologically and numismatically attested before 867 CE, the Shan-derived name Maingmaw is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_mekkhaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 13th century CE and attested as one of the three capitals of the Myinsaing Kingdom from 1297 to 1313 CE.
b_mekkhaya.etymology_analysis: Historical Burmese town in Kyaukse District, founded in the 13th century CE and attested in 1297 CE as a Myinsaing co-capital; post-867 CE.

b_yawnghwe.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1359 CE according to Shan and Burmese historical records (with Burmese form Nyaungshwe).
b_yawnghwe.etymology_analysis: Shan toponym Yawng Hwe (adapted into Burmese as Nyaungshwe). Founded in 1359 CE, post-867 CE.
